title: Time-sliced chunking and sparse KV hierarchy proposal
summary: A proposal for a complementary approach to existing length-bucketing/padding strategies: time-sliced chunking (windowed chunking of long sequences) combined with a sparse multi-tier KV cache. The design targets high tail-latency reduction, improved packing efficiency for mixed-length workloads, and manageable KV memory growth across many concurrent sessions.
content:
Background
There are two painful trade-offs when serving workloads with mixed sequence lengths: wasted compute from padding short requests to long batched shapes, and unbounded KV cache growth when many long-context sessions are active. Existing approaches (length bucketing, mini-buckets, progressive padding) help but still struggle when workloads contain many medium-length tails and when prefix reuse is sparse.

Goals
- Reduce token-level compute waste for mixed-length traffic while preserving low p50/p95 latency.
- Bound KV memory growth without losing high-hit-rate caching for frequently reused prefixes.
- Provide kernel-friendly execution shapes to enable fused/windowed attention kernels.
- Integrate cleanly with scheduling and autoscaling policies.

Key idea: Time-sliced chunking
Instead of always treating the full request sequence as a single continuous attention pass, we split long requests into time-sliced chunks (overlapping windows) for the purpose of packing and execution. Each chunk is a contiguous token window of size W with overlap O between adjacent chunks (e.g., W=512, O=64). Chunks are scheduled as first-class units for batching and kernel selection.
Benefits:
- Short and medium requests naturally map to 1 chunk, reducing padding to power-of-two or kernel-friendly shapes.
- Long requests get processed chunk-by-chunk; early chunks can be returned to the caller while later chunks stream incremental outputs.
- Kernel selection simplifies: choose a fixed-window attention kernel for chunk execution, plus a small number of tail kernels for final partial-chunks.
- Packing: mix many different user requests into chunk-level batches; chunk sizes are uniform so packing efficiency improves versus variable-length sequence packing.

Sparse multi-tier KV hierarchy
We propose a 2-tier KV cache per model shard:
- Hot cache (dense, fast on-device): contains short prefixes and very recent entries; strict LRU/segmented LRU with small per-session caps.
- Warm cache (sparse, compressed indices): a probabilistic/approximate index stored in GPU/CPU off-device memory that points to entries archived in a global compressed store (quantized/hashed).
Behavior:
- On chunk boundaries, allow selective KV snapshotting: only store KV states at chunk-level checkpoints (every K tokens) instead of per-token. That reduces KV cardinality by ~K.
- Promote frequently reused checkpoints to hot cache; evict infrequently accessed ones to warm tier.
- Warm tier supports best-effort retrieval with slightly higher latency but prevents full recomputation of large prefix contexts.

Scheduler and orchestration implications
- Scheduler views tasks as chunk inference jobs with attributes: chunk-length, overlap, priority (latency vs throughput), and KV checkpoint id.
- Use microburst windows: collect incoming chunk tasks for a short collection time (e.g., 2-5 ms) to improve batch sizes but with a deadline-aware constraint so latency SLOs are honored.
- When KV warm-tier hits occur, scheduler may choose slower device or CPU-assisted retrieval path; fallbacks for warm misses trigger re-computation of the preceding chunk using smaller window kernels.

Kernel selection strategy
- Primary kernel family: fixed-window self-attention optimized for W (e.g., W in {256,512,1024}). These kernels are fused and highly throughput-efficient.
- Tail kernel family: partial-window kernels for ends of sequences and overlap merging.
- KV merge kernel: lightweight routine to stitch KV checkpoints when a session requires a long-range reconstruction (best-effort, pipelined with subsequent chunks).
- During scheduling, pick kernel based on chunk_size and whether the hot KV checkpoint is present. If warm-tier only, prefer a kernel that tolerates higher KV fetch latency (asynchronous KV prefetch).

Trade-offs and failure modes
- Consistency/semantics: chunking changes how attention is computed over long-range context. Overlap O must be sufficient to capture cross-window dependencies; for highly global attention workloads, chunking may degrade quality. Mitigation: adaptive O based on model sensitivity metrics, and optional full-prefix recompute for flagged sessions.
- Latency amplification: chunk boundaries add orchestration overhead and potential extra round-trips for clients that expect single-response semantics. Mitigation: streaming-first API and server-side assembly of early outputs.
- KV staleness: checkpointing reduces KV resolution; applications relying on fine-grained per-token KV may see regressions. Provide a per-route config to opt out.

Metrics and experiments to run
- Packing efficiency (tokens executed / tokens requested) across mixed-length synthetic and production traces.
- p50/p95/p99 latency with and without chunking; per-route SLO compliance.
- KV memory usage and hit rate across hot/warm tiers; cost per active session.
- Quality degradation measured by eval prompts designed to stress long-range dependencies (ROUGE/BLEU and model-specific logits delta).

Rollout plan
- Phase 0: offline experiments (simulator that replays traces and evaluates packing + KV size).
- Phase 1: opt-in internal traffic for lower-risk model families; expose chunking configs through per-route flags.
- Phase 2: gated gradual rollout with observability: model quality regression alerts, KV-hit dashboards, and kernel-level perf counters.
- Phase 3: production-wide safe defaults with per-tenant overrides.

Open questions and next steps
- How to pick overlap O adaptively per model/route? Investigate learned heuristics from attention head sensitivity.
- Compression/representation format for warm-tier checkpoint indices (hashing, PQ, or learned quantization).
- API semantics for streaming chunked responses vs single-shot calls; developer ergonomics and SDK changes.
- Cost model: quantify GPU time saved vs additional orchestration and warm-tier retrieval costs.

Appendix: quick spec sketches
- Chunk metadata: {route_id, session_id, chunk_id, checkpoint_id, is_final_chunk, overlap_size} (transport-level compact encoding).
- Default params to test: W=512, O=64, checkpoint_every_K=128, hot_cache_cap_per_session=3.
- Suggested dashboard panels: chunk-level batching rate, per-chunk avg tokens/batch, KV hot-hit rate, warm-retrieval latency distribution.

Notes: This approach is intended to complement (not replace) existing bucketing and padding mechanisms. For many mixed workloads the combination of chunk uniformity + sparse checkpointing leads to substantially better packing and bounded KV growth.

Authors: Asha Patel (primary), Marcus Lee, Sofia Martinez, Ethan Zhao
